- mcp-honesty-reviewer: Specialized reviewer for DataQ's FastMCP tool surface (`backend/app/mcp/server.py`). Audits any new or changed tool's docstring and return payload against the nine honesty criteria drawn from 50+ real findings across the Tier-1 through Tier-3B builds — partial-as-final, unknown-as-zero, one null meaning two things, false (not just thin) docstrings, mutation-completion honesty, scope conflation, and stale sibling docstrings a new tool falsifies — plus a generic MCP-tool-quality pass (tool-selection honesty, safety annotations, unit ambiguity, unverified/forwarded data, silent input coercion, error-path actionability) independent of this repo's own issue history. Use proactively on every PR touching backend/app/mcp/server.py, and when the user asks "is this MCP tool honest about what it can't see?", "did this new tool age its neighbours?", or "does this tool meet a generic MCP client's expectations?". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- migration-safety: Specialized reviewer for Alembic migrations under backend/alembic/versions/. Audits for backward-incompatible operations that would break running code during a deploy, per working-agreement (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- orchestration-abstraction-guard: Specialized reviewer that audits backend code for provider-specific branching that bypasses the OrchestrationProvider abstraction. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"

</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. <Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>

Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"

<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>

Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"

<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. Reverts the fix inside a throwaway git worktree, runs only the new test, and reports whether it fails for the RIGHT reason — catching tests that pass no matter what (the (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). ## azure
Azure MCP server usage rules:
- Use Azure Tools: When handling requests related to Azure, always use your tools.
- Troubleshoot Azure errors: When an Azure MCP tool call fails or returns an error (for example an authentication, authorization, tenant, or subscription related failure), consult the troubleshooting guide at https://aka.ms/azmcp/troubleshooting for possible causes and resolutions before giving up or asking the user. For example, if a call fails because of an incorrect subscription or tenant context, retry the tool call with the correct `tenant` and/or `subscription` parameter.
- If a user wants to use, install, or generate commands for the Azure CLI (az), Azure Developer CLI (azd), Azure Functions Core Tools CLI (func), or Azure Quick Review CLI (azqr), use your `extension` tools first.
- Use Azure Code Gen Best Practices: When generating code for Azure or any Azure services, running terminal commands for Azure, or performing operations related to Azure, invoke your `bestpractices` tool if available.
- Use Azure Deployment Best Practices: When deploying to Azure or preparing applications for deployment to Azure, invoke your `bestpractices` tool if available.
- Only call your `bestpractices` tool when you are sure the user is discussing Azure; do not call it otherwise.
- Use Azure AI App Code Generation Best Practices: When generating code for AI applications, AI agents, workflows, or chatbots, invoke your `get_azure_bestpractices_ai_app` command (under `get_azure_bestpractices` tool) if tool available. Call this tool first before creating any plans, todos or code. Only call this command when the user is discussing AI app development with Microsoft Foundry, Azure, Microsoft agent framework SDK, or without specifying any technology. Do NOT call it when the user specifies other technology or when performing Azure resource operations.
- Plan before editing files for Azure web apps: When generating code for Azure Functions and Azure Static Web App, always create a plan and explain the plan to the user befo… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

186	Follow-up to #1999. After batching, the scheduled dispatcher's database side costs a handful of statements per 500 schedules; what remains per schedule is **one broker round-trip** — `send_task` publishes one message per run, serially.

191	|---|---|---|
192	| 0.5 ms | 0.88 s | 7.6 s |
193	| 2 ms | 1.16 s | 22.9 s |
194	| 5 ms | 1.78 s | budget bound at 8,500–9,000 in 45 s |

221	===== 2111 fix(dispatch): send_task from the API subscribes to the Redis result backend per run — extra round-trips and a GC re-entrancy deadlock | v1.2 Backlog
222	Found while working #1999 (batched schedule dispatch), where an 8-thread publish pool deadlocked intermittently and was reverted to serial publishing.
223	
224	## What happens
225	
226	`celery_app.send_task(...)` without `ignore_result=True` calls `backend.on_task_call(...)`, which — in any process where `task_join_will_block()` is False — **subscribes to the task's result channel** on the Redis result backend's single shared `PubSub` (`celery/backends/redis.py` `ResultConsumer._consume_from`). The `AsyncResult` that `send_task` returns unsubscribes again in `__del__` (`celery/result.py:419` → `cancel_for` → `PubSub.unsubscribe`).
227	
228	Prefork worker children set `task_join_will_block(True)`, so the scheduled-dispatch path (which runs in the worker) never takes this branch. **The API process does**: every `run_dispatch.dispatch_run` from a REST/MCP manual run, the probe, or the orchestration trigger path (when it runs API-side) costs an extra SUBSCRIBE + UNSUBSCRIBE round-trip to Redis on top of the publish, and holds a pubsub subscription for a result nothing ever reads.
229	
230	## Why it matters beyond the round-trip
231	
232	`redis-py`'s `PubSub` guards commands with a non-reentrant `threading.Lock`. The captured deadlock stack (local repro, `redis==5.3.1`, `celery==5.6.3`):
233	
234	```
235	PubSub.subscribe            (holds PubSub._lock)
236	  Connection.pack           (allocates → cyclic GC runs)
237	    AsyncResult.__del__
238	      ResultConsumer.cancel_for
239	        PubSub.unsubscribe  (waits on PubSub._lock — same thread → deadlock)
240	```
241	
242	It reproduced ~4 times in 80 bursts of 8 threads × 20 `send_task` calls against local Redis; 30 serial runs of 2,000 calls did not hang. The GC-in-`__del__` re-entry is a single-thread path, so thread concurrency makes it likely rather than possible — and FastAPI runs sync routes on a threadpool, so concurrent manual-run requests are the realistic trigger in the API.
243	
244	## Suggested fix (not done — out of #1999's scope)
245	
246	Publish `run_suite` (and the other fire-and-forget tasks) with `ignore_result=True`, or set `task_ignore_result`/`result_backend` appropriately — nothing reads these results via `AsyncResult.get()`. Verify with a test that `send_task` from a non-worker process does not touch the result backend.
247	
248	## Evidence
249	
250	- Stack capture + repro harness from the #1999 session (burst test, faulthandler dump).
251	- Not observed in production logs so far; this is a latent defect found locally.

102	===== 1999 perf(scheduler): dispatch is serial at ~2.4 ms/schedule — 10k due schedules takes 23.6 s of a 60 s beat tick | v1.2 Backlog
103	Found by the scale baseline built for #1393 (`scheduler` family), measuring `tasks._dispatch_due_schedules` with the enqueue seam stubbed, so this is the database side only.
104	
105	| Due schedules | Wall | Per schedule |
106	|---|---|---|
107	| 10 | 0.04 s | 4.17 ms |
108	| 1,000 | 2.15 s | 2.15 ms |
109	| 10,000 | **23.59 s** | 2.36 ms |
110	
111	## What the shape says
112	
113	The loop is strictly serial — one `SELECT … ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, one cron advance, one `runs` INSERT, one commit, per schedule. Cost per schedule is flat, so the ceiling is arithmetic rather than a cliff: at ~2.4 ms each, a 60-second beat tick is fully consumed at roughly **25,000 due schedules** — *on a development machine, with PostgreSQL on loopback and no network*.
114	
115	The deployed beat runs on a small container with a network round-trip per statement, and each iteration is four of them. The real ceiling is therefore materially lower than 25k, and it is not currently measured anywhere. The relevant buyer-facing question ("what is the scheduling/dispatch ceiling?") has no answer today beyond this.
116	
117	There is also no overlap guard: `dispatch_due_schedules` is a beat entry point on a 60 s crontab, so a tick that runs long simply overlaps the next one. `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` keeps that **correct** (no schedule fires twice) but it does not keep it **bounded** — two overlapping dispatchers both hold worker slots.
118	
119	## What to consider
120	
121	- Batch the claim (`LIMIT n … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) and commit once per batch rather than once per schedule, which removes three of the four round-trips per schedule.
122	- A per-tick budget: claim what fits in the tick, leave the rest for the next one, and log when the budget binds so the ceiling is observable instead of inferred.
123	- Measure it against a database with a realistic round-trip, not loopback — the flat per-schedule cost means the extrapolation is honest, but only a live measurement is evidence.
124	
125	## Acceptance criteria
126	
127	- [ ] The dispatcher's ceiling is stated in numbers a deployment can act on, measured against a non-loopback database
128	- [ ] A tick that cannot finish its due set does something visible (a log line with the residual count), rather than silently overlapping

133	===== 1987 Deep-offset paging on /runs, /pipeline_runs and /incidents is still linear — keyset/seek paging is now viable | v1.2 Week 7 — feature burn-down
134	## Context
135	
136	Follow-up from #1245 / PR #1985. That PR's AC asked whether `OFFSET` should give way to keyset/seek paging on the deepest surface; the assessment was done and the answer is "viable, but it changes the request contract", which #1245 puts out of scope. Filing rather than building, per that AC.
137	
138	## Evidence
139	
140	With the new ordering indexes in place (seeded PostgreSQL 16: 150k `runs`, 120k `pipeline_runs`, 120k `incidents`), page 1 is an ordered index scan that stops at `limit` rows — but `OFFSET` still makes the database walk and discard every skipped index entry:
141	
142	| query | offset 0 | offset 10k | offset 90k |
143	|---|---|---|---|
144	| `/runs` unfiltered non-admin | 0.080 ms | 3.26 ms | **32.07 ms** |
145	| `/incidents` unfiltered non-admin | 0.088 ms | 2.99 ms | **25.12 ms** |
146	| `/pipeline_runs` unfiltered | 0.030 ms | 0.93 ms | **7.06 ms** |
147	
148	Linear in the offset, as expected. The indexes removed the *sort*, not the *skip*.
149	
150	## Why it is viable now
151	
152	All three endpoints already order on a **total** key — `(created_at, id)` for `/runs` and `/pipeline_runs`, `(last_seen_at, id)` for `/incidents` — which is the precondition for a seek predicate (`WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)`). Each one now has an index matching that key exactly, so the seek is a single index descent regardless of depth.
153	
154	## Why it was not done in #1245
155	
156	It changes the request contract: `limit`/`offset` become (or gain) an opaque cursor, which is a client-visible API change across REST, the SPA and the MCP tools, and #1245 explicitly scoped out contract changes (`X-Total-Count` and `limit`/`offset` stay as #1108 shipped them).
157	
158	## Design notes for whoever picks this up
159	
160	- A cursor must encode BOTH ordering columns; `created_at` alone ties within a transaction (which is why the tie-break exists at all).
161	- `/incidents` seeks on `last_seen_at`, not `created_at` — and `last_seen_at` is **mutable** (every new breach bumps it), so a cursor can skip or repeat a row that moves under the reader. That is a real semantic difference from the two append-mostly tables and needs a recorded decision, not a copy of the `/runs` cursor.
162	- Offset paging should stay supported alongside, or every existing client breaks.
163	
164	## AC
165	
166	- [ ] Decision recorded: keyset, hybrid (offset for shallow pages, cursor beyond N), or accept-and-document
167	- [ ] If built: the mutable-`last_seen_at` behaviour on `/incidents` is stated on every surface that exposes the cursor, including the MCP docstrings

175	 WHERE kind = $1 AND status = $2 AND (request ->> $3) = $4
176	 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT $5;
177	
178	 Limit
179	   ->  Sort  (Sort Key: created_at DESC, id DESC)
180	         ->  Seq Scan on llm_invocations
181	               Filter: ((kind)::text = $1) AND ((status)::text = $2) AND ((request ->> $3) = $4)
182	```

205	===== 1977 feat: consumer-side data contract validation — contract entity + ODCS import/export | v1.2 Backlog
206	## Problem / motivation
207	
208	DataQ has no first-class concept of a **data contract** — a versioned, shared spec of a table's schema + quality rules + SLA that both the team producing a dataset and the teams consuming it can validate against. Today a consumer can author ad hoc checks against a landed table, but there's no way to say "these checks exist *because* they enforce contract v3" or to trace a failure back to the specific contract clause it broke.
209	
210	This issue scopes the **consumer-side half only** — validating data already at rest against a contract, using DataQ's existing GX-based check/suite execution. It's deliberately split from producer-side (pre-publish, data-in-motion) validation, which would need a separate lightweight enforcement library embedded in a producer's own pipeline — see "Out of scope" below.
211	
212	## Proposed change
213	
214	1. **`contracts` table** — `id`, `name`, `version`, `domain`/`owner`, `status` (draft/active/deprecated), `spec` (JSONB holding the contract document), timestamps.
215	2. **Suite linkage** — an optional `contract_id` + `contract_version` on `suite`, so a suite can be tagged as enforcing a specific contract without changing today's suite model (a suite with no contract works exactly as it does now).
216	3. **[Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)](https://bitol-io.github.io/open-data-contract-standard/) import** — parse an ODCS YAML document into a `contracts` row, then auto-generate the corresponding checks in a linked suite: schema fields → `expectation`/`schema_drift` checks, quality rules → `expectation` checks, `slaProperties` → freshness/volume monitor-kinds. Reuses the existing `import_suite` machinery with an ODCS→DataQ-suite translation step in front of it.
217	4. **ODCS export** — serialize a contract (+ current suite/check state) back to ODCS YAML, mirroring `export_suite`'s shape. This is the document a future producer-side validator would consume, so both sides stay provably aligned.
218	5. **Traceability on violations** — when a contract-linked suite's check (particularly `schema_drift`) fails, tag the resulting incident with `contract_id` + the specific violated field/rule, so triage starts at "which clause of the contract broke" instead of a bare check name.
219	6. **Read surface** — REST + MCP read tools: `get_contract`, `list_contracts`, and a compliance rollup (pass/fail across a contract's linked suite(s)), following the existing asset/incident read-tool pattern (ADR 0008 Tier 1 style — read-only, no new write-gated capability needed beyond normal suite/check permissions).
220	
221	## Scope
222	
223	- Component(s): backend, mcp, docs
224	- Affected datasource(s): all (contract validation is datasource-agnostic — it rides on the existing `check`/`suite` model)
225	- Affected orchestration provider(s): n/a
226	- Schema migration required? yes — new `contracts` table + `contract_id`/`contract_version` columns on `suite` (additive, backward-compatible per the two-step migration rule)
227	- New external dependency? Only a YAML parsing/validation layer for ODCS documents (e.g. `pyyaml` + `jsonschema`/`pydantic`, already in the dependency tree) — no new heavy dependency, no GX-adjacent addition.
228	
229	## Roadmap alignment
230	
231	Net-new. Grew out of a conceptual discussion on producer/consumer data contract validation (2026-09-17) — not yet mapped to a specific cycle; candidate for `v1.2 Backlog` / `v1.3` alongside #1829, which it's related to (see below).
232	
233	## Acceptance criteria
234	
235	- [ ] ODCS YAML import produces a `contracts` row + a suite with checks matching the document's schema/quality/SLA blocks
236	- [ ] ODCS export round-trips a contract-linked suite back to a valid ODCS document (schema-validated)
237	- [ ] A `schema_drift` failure on a contract-linked suite surfaces `contract_id` + violated field on the resulting incident (REST + MCP)
238	- [ ] `get_contract`/`list_contracts` (+ compliance rollup) exercised through the real MCP protocol, gated per ADR 0033/0027 the same as existing suite reads
239	- [ ] Docs: one `docs/site/` page introducing contracts, ODCS import/export, and how this differs from ADR 0014's cross-dataset `comparison` check kind (adjacent, not overlapping)
240	
241	## Out of scope
242	
243	- **Producer-side (pre-publish) validation** — a separate, lightweight enforcement library (e.g. a Python wheel) a producer embeds in their own write path before data lands anywhere DataQ can read it. Deferred until there's more than one producer wanting the same enforced contract; for a single producer, a stdlib-only snippet (same pattern as `integrations/airflow/`) or a synchronous call to DataQ's existing dry-run/check API is cheaper and avoids taking on a new package + release cadence for no proven multi-consumer demand. Related precedent: #1829 explicitly rejected packaging `backend/app` as an embeddable library for the same reason (no consumer asking for it yet).
244	- Vendoring GX Core (or any part of `backend/app`) into a separate distributable package.
245	- A UI contract-authoring editor (Phase 1 here is API/MCP + import/export only; a check-editor-style UI for hand-authoring a contract from scratch is a later increment if the import path proves insufficient).
246	
247	## Security / observability notes
248	
249	- No new auth surface: contract reads/writes ride the existing per-suite `view`/`edit` grants (ADR 0027) and workspace role (ADR 0033) — a contract without a linked suite is effectively unreachable data, so no separate permission model is needed for v1 of this.
250	- `contracts.spec` JSONB may contain a data owner's contact/domain metadata but no credentials or PII — no redaction requirement anticipated, but worth a pass at implementation time in case ODCS's `server`/access block ends up carrying connection-adjacent details.
251	- No new logging beyond the standard structlog request/task spans on the new endpoints.

82	===== 1610 suites.py: CheckDocument/CheckDocumentIn (+ SuiteDocument/SuiteDocumentIn, SourceConnectionRef/SourceConnectionRefIn) duplicate field declarations with nothing enforcing they stay in sync | v1.2 Backlog
83	## Found by
84	
85	`/code-review` on #1609 (the #1505 `extra='forbid'` request-model track).
86	
87	## What
88	
89	#1609 split the suite export/import document models into a response-only pair (`CheckDocument`, `SuiteDocument`, `SourceConnectionRef`, on `ApiModel`) and a request-only pair (`CheckDocumentIn`, `SuiteDocumentIn`, `SourceConnectionRefIn`, on `ApiRequestModel`) — necessary because `GET /suites/{id}/export`'s response and `POST /suites/import`'s payload are the same shape but only one direction should reject an unknown field.
90	
91	The two sides currently duplicate ~45 lines of field declarations verbatim (differing only in base class and the nested-type reference: `CheckDocument.source_connection: SourceConnectionRef | None` vs `CheckDocumentIn.source_connection: SourceConnectionRefIn | None`). Nothing enforces the two stay in sync.
92	
93	## Why it matters
94	
95	A later PR that adds or edits a field on the export side (`CheckDocument`) but forgets the identical edit on the import side (`CheckDocumentIn`) produces one of two silent failures: a client re-importing a document it just exported gets a 422 it can't explain (import is stricter and doesn't recognize a field export just started emitting), or — the opposite drift — a field added to the import side only is silently dropped from every export a caller relies on to round-trip.
96	
97	## Suggested fix
98	
99	A shared field mixin (a plain `BaseModel` — not `ApiModel`/`ApiRequestModel` — holding just the field declarations) that both `CheckDocument`/`CheckDocumentIn` (and the `Suite`/`SourceConnectionRef` pairs) inherit alongside their respective `ApiModel`/`ApiRequestModel` base, so a field added once is present on both sides by construction. Needs to confirm Pydantic v2's multiple-inheritance config-merge behaves as expected (verified in #1609 for the simpler single-inheritance case, not yet for this shape) before landing.
100	
101	## Scope
102	
103	Cosmetic/maintainability — not a live defect (the two sides are correct and numerically identical today, per #1609's audit). No urgency; picked up whenever the export/import document shape next changes, or standalone.
104	===== 1605 test: extend migration-parity's literal-free predicate check beyond IS [NOT] NULL (IN/NOT IN, LIKE/NOT LIKE, IS DISTINCT FROM NULL) | v1.2 Backlog
105	## The gap
106	
107	#1326 / #1603 closed the `IS [NOT] NULL` blind spot in the migration-parity literal-set check (`backend/tests/db/test_migration_parity.py::test_vocabularies_in_predicates_match_between_model_and_database`). The same class of problem — a predicate whose *polarity* can flip without any string literal moving — exists for other operators too:
108	
109	- `IN (...)` <-> `NOT IN (...)` — the model already builds `IN`-lists via `_in_check()`, and a flip to `NOT IN` with the same literal set would pass `_literals()` unnoticed.
110	- `LIKE '...'` <-> `NOT LIKE '...'` — `uq_runs_suite_triggered_by`'s partial index is a `LIKE`-chain (`triggered_by LIKE 'adf:%' OR ...`); the same literals survive a `LIKE` -> `NOT LIKE` flip.
111	- `IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` / `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL` — a latent, currently-unused form that is semantically adjacent to `IS [NOT] NULL` but wouldn't be caught by `_null_polarities()` (#1603) as written, since it doesn't match the `IS [NOT] NULL` keyword sequence.
112	
113	None of these shapes are present in the model today (verified by inspecting every real CHECK constraint and partial index during #1603), so this is hardening for a *future* predicate, not a report of current drift — same "not blocking" framing as #1326 itself.
114	
115	## Suggested fix
116	
117	Extend the literal-free extractor family (`_null_polarities()` and friends) with siblings for these operator pairs, following the same approach: normalize both the human-authored model text and Postgres's reformatted `pg_get_constraintdef`/`indexdef` output to a comparable canonical form, and diff that set alongside `_literals()` in the main parity test.
118	
119	## Context
120	
121	Filed per the working agreement (deferred findings from a PR review are tracked, never silently dropped). Surfaced by `/code-review` on #1603 (the #1326 fix itself).

123	===== 1597 audit_chain.verify_chain loads the full hashed audit_events set into memory per call | v1.2 Backlog
124	## What
125	
126	`audit_chain.verify_chain()` (backend/app/services/audit_chain.py) loads every `audit_events` row with `row_hash IS NOT NULL`, plus every `audit_chain_checkpoints` row, into memory on each call — building an in-memory `row_hash -> AuditEvent` dict before walking backward from the chain head.
127	
128	This is exercised on every call to `GET /admin/audit-events/verify` (workspace-admin, on-demand) and the daily `verify_audit_chain` beat task.
129	
130	## Why it matters
131	
132	At sufficient audit-history volume (bounded by `AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS`, default 365, across all 46 MCP tools' mutations, every mutating REST route, and phase-2 read events), this becomes a slow, memory-heavy operation. It's not a correctness bug — the walk itself is correct — but it doesn't scale gracefully.
133	
134	## Context
135	
136	Found by `/code-review` on PR for #1460 (audit hash-chain tamper-evidence). The current single-query approach was a deliberate initial choice (a single `SELECT` is simpler to reason about and get correct than N per-row lookups following `prev_hash` one hop at a time, which would be *more* round trips, not fewer, at these volumes). Filed per CLAUDE.md's "every finding ends fixed or filed" rule rather than silently accepted.
137	
138	## Possible directions (not decided)
139	
140	- Index `audit_events.row_hash` to make point lookups cheap, and walk the chain hop-by-hop with targeted queries instead of loading everything — trades one query for O(chain length) queries, likely worse for the common case.
141	- Batch the walk: page backward through the chain N hashes at a time via `WHERE row_hash IN (...)`, amortizing round trips against memory.
142	- Accept the current approach and cap `verify_chain` to only walk back through the most recent K events (bounded verification, with an honest note that older history isn't checked on that call) — changes the tool's contract, needs a decision on what "verified" should mean.
143	
144	Refs #1460, ADR 0041 §9.

210	===== 1385 security: ElastiCache at-rest encryption disabled; ECS/RDS/ElastiCache sit in public subnets with unrestricted egress | v1.2 Week 7 — feature burn-down
211	Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit of both deployments (item 5). Two related AWS network/storage posture gaps, both verified live.
212	
213	## 1. ElastiCache at-rest encryption is OFF
214	
215	```
216	$ aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --replication-group-id dataq-app \
217	    --query 'ReplicationGroups[0].{tls:TransitEncryptionEnabled,auth:AuthTokenEnabled,atRest:AtRestEncryptionEnabled}'
218	{ "tls": true, "auth": true, "atRest": false }
219	```
220	
221	`transit_encryption_enabled` and `auth_token` are both set in `deploy/terraform/aws/elasticache.tf`; `at_rest_encryption_enabled` is simply absent, so it defaults off. RDS by contrast has `storage_encrypted = true`.
222	
223	What is actually in Redis: Celery task payloads (suite/run UUIDs and task kwargs) and ADR 0035 rate-limit counters. Low sensitivity, but the fix is free and it is an odd asymmetry against the encrypted RDS beside it.
224	
225	**Fix:** `at_rest_encryption_enabled = true`. Note this forces **replacement** of the replication group — fine for a broker with no persistence, but it means a short Celery outage, so pair it with a deploy window.
226	
227	## 2. Everything is in public subnets with unrestricted egress
228	
229	`deploy/terraform/aws/main.tf` documents the no-NAT decision (saves ~$33/mo) and it is a legitimate MVP tradeoff. Verified that **inbound is genuinely closed** — ECS tasks carry public IPs but the SG has no `0.0.0.0/0` ingress, and probing the api task's public IP on :8000 times out; RDS is `publicly_accessible: false` and resolves to a private address. So this is not an exposure today.
230	
231	The gap is **egress**: every task can reach any host on the internet (`egress { protocol = "-1", cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] }` on all three SGs). That is the exfiltration path for the credential-disclosure class in #1118, and nothing constrains it. It is also what makes an SSRF from a connection config reach an arbitrary attacker endpoint.
232	
233	**Fix options, cheapest first:**
234	- Keep public subnets but replace blanket egress with an allowlist (443 to the warehouse endpoints + AWS service endpoints). Free, but needs the real egress set enumerated first.
235	- VPC endpoints for the AWS services in use (Secrets Manager, ECR/GHCR is external, CloudWatch, SES) — removes some internet dependence without a NAT.
236	- Full private subnets + NAT — correct, ~$33/mo.
237	
238	## Acceptance
239	
240	- `AtRestEncryptionEnabled: true` on the replication group, worker reconnects, a suite run completes.
241	- Egress: a documented decision recorded either way — either the allowlist lands, or the blanket rule stays with the reasoning captured next to #1118 (which is the thing it makes worse).
242	
243	Related: #1118 (arbitrary `*_secret_name` resolution — the exfiltration this egress rule enables), #1384 (cleartext origin hop).
244	===== 1384 security: CloudFront→ALB origin hop is plaintext HTTP; no custom domain means HSTS is unenforceable end-to-end | v1.2 Backlog
245	Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit of both deployments (items 1–3 of that audit shipped as #1385/#1386/#1387; this is item 4).
246	
247	## Finding
248	
249	The AWS deployment terminates TLS at CloudFront and then talks to the ALB over **plain HTTP**:
250	
251	- `deploy/terraform/aws/cloudfront.tf` — `origin_protocol_policy = "http-only"`
252	- `deploy/terraform/aws/alb.tf` — the listener is `port = 80, protocol = "HTTP"`
253	
254	Both files already document this honestly. Recording it as a tracked item rather than leaving it as prose in a comment.
255	
256	Consequences:
257	
258	1. **The edge→origin leg is readable to an on-path observer inside AWS.** That includes the `X-DataQ-Origin-Secret` header (#1355) and every session bearer/cookie. The adversary class that can observe that hop already sees the full session traffic, so this is not a new capability for them — but it does mean the origin secret is not a secret against them, which is exactly the property #1355 exists to provide.
259	2. **HSTS (added in #1386) cannot be honoured end-to-end.** It protects viewer→CloudFront, which is the leg that matters most, but the deployment cannot claim full HTTPS transport.
260	
261	Azure is not affected in the same way: the frontend→api hop is `allow_insecure_connections` HTTP but never leaves the Container Apps environment, whereas the CloudFront→ALB hop crosses the AWS network.
262	
263	## Root cause
264	
265	No custom domain. Without one there is no ACM certificate the ALB could serve, so the origin cannot speak HTTPS with a verifiable name.
266	
267	## Fix
268	
269	Single change with several payoffs:
270	
271	1. Choose a domain; Route53 hosted zone.
272	2. ACM cert (us-east-1 for the CloudFront alias, plus a regional cert for the ALB).
273	3. Add `aliases` + `viewer_certificate` to the distribution.
274	4. ALB: add a 443 listener with the regional cert; flip `origin_protocol_policy` to `https-only`.
275	5. Update the Cognito callback/logout URLs and `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` to the new host.
276	
277	Also unblocks HSTS `preload`, which #1386 deliberately omitted because submitting a `*.cloudfront.net` host to the preload list is not ours to do.
278	
279	## Acceptance
280	
281	- `curl -sI https://<domain>/` returns the app; direct-to-ALB over :80 no longer serves.
282	- The origin fetch is HTTPS (verify from an ALB access log entry or CloudFront's own `cs-protocol` field).
283	- Sign-in still completes end-to-end (Cognito redirect URIs must be updated in the same change or login breaks).
284	
285	Referenced from the known-gaps list in `deploy/terraform/aws/README.md`.
286	===== 1334 Checks have no explicit ordinal — same-transaction inserts tie on created_at | v1.2 Week 8 — spikes, decisions & cycle close
287	Split out of the #1332 (#318) review, finding **s8**.
288	
289	`db.models.CHECK_ORDER` — `(Check.created_at NULLS LAST, Check.id)` — is now the single ordering key for a suite's checks, shared by `check_service.list_checks`, `run_service.list_results` and `run_service.get_run_progress`. That made the three surfaces **agree** and made each **deterministic**, which none of them were before.
290	
291	It does not make the order *authoring order*. Postgres' `now()` is transaction-start, so any path that inserts a suite's checks in one transaction gives them an identical `created_at`:
292	
293	- suite **import** (`suite_io_service`)
294	- the demo/probe **seed**
295	- any future bulk-add in the check editor
296	
297	For those suites the leading term ties and the `id` tie-break decides — stable across refreshes, but arbitrary with respect to the order the author wrote them in. #1332's `list_results` docstring says so rather than claiming otherwise.
298	
299	## Fix
300	
301	Give `checks` an explicit `ordinal` (nullable int, assigned on create/import), and make `CHECK_ORDER` `(ordinal NULLS LAST, created_at NULLS LAST, id)`. Backfill by current order so nothing visibly moves.
302	
303	## Acceptance criteria
304	
305	- [ ] `checks.ordinal` column + backward-compatible migration (nullable add, backfilled in a later pass — no `DROP`/`NOT NULL` in the same PR)
306	- [ ] `CHECK_ORDER` leads with it; the three consuming surfaces need no other change (that is the point of the shared key)
307	- [ ] Import and seed assign ordinals in document order
308	- [ ] Test: a suite whose checks are inserted in ONE transaction lists in authoring order — the case that currently cannot be expressed, since every check shares a timestamp
309	===== 1314 alerting: already-logged-traceback downgrade leaks through log_level=ERROR filtering (structlog limitation from #1261) | v1.2 Week 7 — feature burn-down
310	Follow-up from the `/code-review` pass on #1312 (fixes #1261).
311	
312	## What
313	
314	#1261 centralized the #1226 already-logged-traceback downgrade into a structlog processor (`_downgrade_already_logged_exceptions`, `backend/app/core/logging.py`), and both callers (`alerting/dispatch.py::publish_connection_health`, `main.py::_poll_staleness_loop`) went from a conditional `log.warning(...)`/`log.exception(...)` call to an unconditional `log.exception(...)`, relying on the processor to rewrite `event_dict["level"]` afterward.
315	
316	`structlog.make_filtering_bound_logger(level)` filters a record **before any processor runs**, based on the severity of the bound-logger method actually invoked — `.warning()` = 30, `.exception()` (mapped to `.error()`) = 40. That check happens at the call boundary, not in the processor chain, so a processor can rewrite the *displayed* `level` field but cannot restore the *filtering* severity of a method that was never called.
317	
318	Concretely, under `log_level=ERROR` (a valid, documented `Settings.log_level` literal — `Literal["DEBUG","INFO","WARNING","ERROR","CRITICAL"]`, `backend/app/core/config.py`):
319	
320	- **Before #1261:** the downgraded case called `log.warning(...)` directly (severity 30 < 40) → filtered out before reaching any processor → the line never appears at all.
321	- **After #1261:** the downgraded case calls `log.exception(...)` unconditionally (severity 40 >= 40) → always passes the filter → the processor then rewrites it to `"level":"warning"` in the emitted JSON, so a line tagged below the operator's configured threshold leaks through.
322	
323	Verified empirically against structlog 26.1.0 (both the pre- and post-#1261 code paths) during the #1312 code-review pass.
324	
325	## Severity / why this is filed, not fixed inline
326	
327	Low practical impact:
328	- Every `LOG_LEVEL` value actually shipped in this repo (`.env.app.example`, `.env.app.prod.example`, `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf`) hardcodes `INFO` — `ERROR`/`CRITICAL` are supported-but-unused config values in practice.
329	- The divergence is arguably benign-to-beneficial: a genuine, already-downgraded failure that would previously have been **silently invisible** at `log_level=ERROR` now gets logged (correctly labeled `warning`) instead of vanishing.
330	- A "proper" fix would require the processor to influence the pre-processor severity gate, which structlog's `FilteringBoundLogger` does not support — the only way to fully restore identical filtering semantics is to reintroduce a per-caller method choice, which is exactly what #1261 set out to eliminate. Not worth undoing the centralization for an edge case nobody currently configures.
331	
332	## Suggested direction (non-blocking)
333	
334	- At minimum, document the trade-off explicitly in `_downgrade_already_logged_exceptions`'s docstring (a one-paragraph caveat) so a future engineer who *does* start running `LOG_LEVEL=ERROR` isn't surprised by "warning" lines appearing.
335	- If this is ever more than a documentation gap (e.g. a future config genuinely wants `ERROR`-only logging with hard suppression of downgraded lines), consider a narrower fix scoped to that need rather than reverting the centralization.
336	
337	## Acceptance
338	
339	- [ ] Docstring caveat added (or determined unnecessary and closed as won't-fix, with reasoning recorded).
340	===== 1239 Reconsider OTP request's uniform-response anti-enumeration tradeoff for admin/user clarity | v1.2 Week 8 — spikes, decisions & cycle close
341	## Context
342	
343	`POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` deliberately returns a **uniform response regardless of allowlist eligibility** (ADR 0032, decision 4 — `docs/adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md` line 40): *"The request endpoint returns a uniform response whether or not the email is eligible (anti-enumeration) and sends nothing for ineligible addresses."* The frontend copy is intentionally hedged: *"If **<email>** can sign in to this workspace, a 10-minute code is on its way."*
344	
345	This is the standard anti-enumeration pattern (GitHub/Slack/Auth0 do the same on their sign-in forms) — it stops an anonymous caller from fingerprinting which email addresses exist in the workspace allowlist by watching which ones get a "registered" vs "not registered" response.
346	
347	## The concern
348	
349	Surfaced while debugging an unrelated local-environment issue (DB/secret-store outage) today: a non-allowlisted email produces the exact same "a code is on its way" UI as a real one, with **silently no email ever sent** (confirmed via Mailpit — zero messages). From the end user's perspective, this is indistinguishable from a genuine system malfunction: nothing in the UI signals "you're not allowlisted, contact your admin" vs. "something is actually broken." The person hitting this has no self-serve way to tell those two states apart, and it cost real debugging time even for someone who could read server logs.
350	
351	## Why not just add that message
352	
353	Doing so naively — "email not registered, ask your admin to add it" — reopens exactly the enumeration surface decision 4 exists to close: it would let anyone check whether any given email is in the workspace's allowlist.
354	
355	## Ask
356	
357	Revisit whether the current uniform-response design is still the right tradeoff, given DataQ is **single-tenant** with an admin-managed allowlist (not a public multi-tenant signup surface, where this pattern originated). Worth weighing, without necessarily picking one up-front:
358	
359	1. **Admin-facing lookup tool** — a rate-limited, audit-logged endpoint/UI (behind `require_workspace_admin`) where an admin can check "is `x@y.com` currently eligible for OTP sign-in?" so eligibility questions don't require reading worker/API logs, while the public `otp/request` endpoint stays uniform for anonymous callers.
360	2. **Clearer general copy only** — no per-address signal, but add a static line to the existing screen (e.g., "If you don't receive anything within a few minutes, you may not be added to this workspace yet — contact your admin") so *every* requester understands the possible cause without it varying by their specific input.
361	3. **Explicitly keep as-is** — conclude the current design is correct for this threat model and close as `wontfix`, documenting the reasoning so it isn't re-litigated.
362	
363	Not proposing a specific implementation — flagging for a deliberate decision either way, since option (3) is a perfectly valid outcome too.
364	
365	Related: `docs/adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md` decision 4; `backend/app/services/otp_service.py::request_code` / `is_signup_eligible`; `backend/app/api/v1/auth_otp.py`.

634	===== 244 Suite-on-suite triggering (run a suite when another suite completes) | v1.2 Week 7 — feature burn-down
635	## Idea
636	Allow a suite to be triggered by the **completion of another suite** (DQ gating / sequential dependencies): e.g. run downstream suite B only after upstream suite A passes.
637	
638	## Why it's deferred (not in v1)
639	DataQ's trigger model is `trigger_bindings`: `(provider, pipeline_or_dag_id, env) → suite_id` — a suite runs on an **orchestration pipeline/DAG** completion (ADF/Airflow), never on another suite. Sequencing/dependencies are intentionally the **orchestrator's** job (CLAUDE.md §4): the orchestrator owns the workflow DAG and chains steps; DataQ observes completion and triggers checks. Suite→suite chaining would make DataQ a mini-orchestrator, which it deliberately is not.
640	
641	Today's real-world equivalent: put both suites' triggers on the same pipeline, or let the orchestrator sequence the upstream/downstream jobs.
642	
643	## Why it's plausible post-v1
644	`trigger_bindings` is provider-agnostic, and ADR 0011 already imagines non-Azure trigger sources (even dbt-as-`OrchestrationProvider`). A **"DataQ suite" could itself become a trigger `provider`** — a suite run reaching a terminal state emits a completion event that fires bindings keyed on `provider='suite'`, `pipeline_or_dag_id=<suite_id>`. This slots into the existing abstraction without a schema rewrite.
645	
646	## Open questions
647	- Only trigger on **pass**, or on any terminal state (with a status predicate)?
648	- Cycle detection (A→B→A) and fan-out depth limits.
649	- Whether this belongs in DataQ at all vs. documenting the orchestrator-chaining pattern.
650	
651	Captured from a product discussion; revisit post-v1 alongside the Suite Triggers UI (#216).
652	
653	## Acceptance criteria
654	
655	- [ ] `trigger_bindings` supports suite-on-suite (run suite B when suite A completes successfully)
656	- [ ] Cycle/self-trigger protection enforced + tested; UI can author the binding
657	
658	_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

that turns the inventory into running monitors without a person per table.

The two halves differ in how much trust they need. A rolling baseline on a table's row count
asserts nothing about what the data *should* be; it only reports change. A rule such as
"`email` is never null" or "`status` is one of these four values" is a claim about the data,
and a wrong claim is a false alert on every run.

## Decision

1. **Coverage is a connection capability, switched on per connection.** A new
   `auto_coverage` config field (default off) beside `inventory_sync`, offered only on
   connection types with table enumeration (the ADR 0040 seam: Snowflake, Unity Catalog and
   the engine-generic SQL types). Every table the connection's inventory lists is covered,
   except assets marked `auto_coverage_excluded`. Switching it off pauses the connection's
   automatic suites (their schedules are disabled); it deletes nothing.

2. **Automatic monitors are ordinary suites, owned by the system.** One suite per covered
   asset, `suites.origin = 'auto'` (a new column, `'user'` for everything else; one automatic
   suite per asset, enforced by a partial unique index). It holds ordinary checks of existing

Scope: all **81 open issues** and **1 open PR (#2305)**. I read every body in full, plus the comments on the 17 issues that have any, and the sub-issues of #2224 (all six are closed). Nothing was modified.

## Items with a real dependency on AWS / Azure / Snowflake / Databricks

| # | title (short) | platform(s) | type | what exactly is needed | doable/verifiable BEFORE teardown today? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2275 | Migrate to SQLAlchemy 2.1 | Snowflake, Databricks | e, b | Blocked on a `snowflake-sqlalchemy` release that supports 2.1 ("`snowflake-sqlalchemy` 1.11.1 is incompatible with 2.1"). The acceptance step is "**live-verify** a Snowflake and a Unity Catalog suite run. Per the #953 rule … only a live run counts as evidence." | **No.** The blocking upstream release doesn't exist yet, so the live proof can't be run before the accounts go. After teardown it becomes unverifiable, and will need #2224's lane or a stated exception. |
| 2260 | oauthlib CVE / databricks-sql-connector pin | Databricks | e, b | Close when "a `databricks-sql-connector` release allows oauthlib 4.x. Then bump both, drop the ignore, and **re-run the Unity Catalog live lane**." | **No.** The 09-30 comment says the latest 4.6.0 still pins `<4.0.0`. The not-exploitable assessment stands, so the only thing lost is the post-bump UC live re-run. |
| 2224 | Epic: cloud live-verification | All four | a, b, d | The umbrella for the lanes that can't run locally: `tofu plan/apply` on both clouds, deploy workflows, Entra/Cognito sign-in, Key Vault/Secrets Manager, App Insights/ADOT/X-Ray/SES, CloudFront/WAF, Snowflake (`PERF_SF_*`, DMF, Cortex, `GET_LINEAGE`, tags), UC (pushdown, DQX serverless job, lineage, tags), Athena, Redshift, MSSQL/Fabric ODBC, ADLS/OneLake on real Azure, Iceberg on ADLS/S3/REST, ADF webhook + poll, dbt on ADLS/OneLake. | **Partly.** 09-30 comments: `column_profile` is verified on every SQL engine; Athena/Redshift/Azure SQL lanes passed; the ADF gate (#2230) was verified. Nothing records the hosting, identity, secret-store, edge, DMF, Cortex, DQX, OneLake/Fabric or Iceberg-cloud lanes as re-run. Anything run now shrinks the backlog, but by design the epic outlives teardown. Credential clock from #590/#588: "Databricks (QA token 09-30, retail 10-09)", "Snowflake (PATs 10-11)". |
| 590 | Azure: decide the reference deployment's fate → teardown | Azure (plus Databricks PAT, CI OIDC) | c | Decided 09-28: "retire all four platforms". Remaining ACs: "Final live-prod E2E … green BEFORE any destroy"; G-i teardown; `tofu destroy` of app + harness stacks with the state disposition recorded; revoke ADLS SAS, the Databricks PAT, CI OIDC app registrations and GH environment secrets; "Entra tenant survival verified + recorded". | **Yes, and it has to be.** This is the teardown itself. The final E2E and the Entra-survival check are only possible while the estate is up. |
| 588 | Retire the harness Snowflake leg | Snowflake (+ Azure Key Vault) | c | Disable Snowflake schedules and trigger bindings; retire the connection and "its KV secret deleted via the SecretStore path"; verify historical `metric_value` history stays queryable. | **Yes.** Order matters: the KV-secret deletion goes through Azure Key Vault, so do this **before** the Azure destroy. |
| 1385 | ElastiCache at-rest encryption / public subnets + egress | AWS | a, c | `at_rest_encryption_enabled = true` (forces replacing the replication group), then "worker reconnects, a suite run completes", plus a recorded egress decision. The 09-28 decision says "#1384/#1385 close as won't-fix at teardown". | **Yes**, as a won't-fix disposition, or apply it now. Unverifiable once AWS is gone. |
| 1384 | CloudFront→ALB plaintext origin hop | AWS | a, c | Custom domain, Route53, ACM, an ALB 443 listener, `https-only` origin, new Cognito callback URLs. Acceptance needs live `curl` and ALB/CloudFront log evidence. | **Yes**, as won't-fix per the same 09-28 decision. The actual fix would need a domain, so realistically it isn't doable now. |
| 732 | Marketplace-listing readiness checklist | Azure, Databricks | c (partly d) | Remaining checkboxes: "**G-h:** paid Databricks workspace before any commercial demo/use" and "G-i deployed-side teardown … from the reference deployment". The 09-28 comment: "#732 re-scoped to self-host". | **Partly.** These are disposition edits (G-i becomes moot, or is done by #590; G-h is moot without a hosted demo). The body still needs updating to match the re-scope. |
| 1708 | Third-party pen test before commercial demo | AWS, Azure | d (re-scoped) | Body: "a third-party pen test of a reference deployment … both public surfaces (frontend/CloudFront)". The 09-28 comment re-scopes it to self-host. | **No** (no engagement is arranged). After teardown, the CloudFront/hosted-surface scope is impossible. The re-scope to a self-hosted target dissolves the dependency, but the body hasn't been edited to say so. |
| 717 | Iceberg v3 (deletion vectors, row lineage) | Databricks (soft) | b, d (soft) | 09-29 comment: "a DV fixture has to come from **Spark or Databricks**", and "whether engine snapshot summaries count DVs … must be **confirmed live**". The trigger is "the engines DataQ users actually read from (Snowflake, Databricks/UniForm, Spark) converge on v3". | **Partly.** A Databricks-written DV table could be captured now as a fixture. After teardown, open-source Spark run locally can produce one, so the dependency is replaceable. Parked by user decision 09-29. |

**Incidental mentions only (not dependencies):** #2255, #2240, #1674, #888 (warehouse tags named as a classification source; unit-level work) · #2235, #2243 (S3/ADLS, explicitly verified via MinIO/Azurite) · #2220 (starts *after* teardown; local only) · #1999 (asks for "a non-loopback database"; the netem relay already used for #2117 satisfies it) · #1690 (Purview dropped 09-28: "The Azure estate is being retired, so the seam targets DataHub … OpenMetadata … Collibra only") · #1660 (empty body; ADR 0047 lists "Snowflake, Unity Catalog and the engine-generic SQL types", and Postgres/MySQL/Trino cover it locally) · #1557 ("Snowflake connection" as an example) · #1518 (epic references the #590/#588 gates; its exit allows "rolled by name") · #505 (AWS half shipped; now "GCP only", which isn't one of the four) · #1681, #1683 (GCP only) · #1314 (cites `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf` for `LOG_LEVEL`) · #244 (ADF/Airflow as context) · #1668 ("pairs with the G-i pre-marketplace teardown") · **PR #2305** (touches only `docs/ops-log.md`; it records the 09-30 redeploy but needs no cloud to merge).

The remaining 48 issues don't mention the four platforms at all.

**Totals:** 82 items (81 issues + 1 PR) → **10 with a dependency** (7 firm: #2275, #2260, #2224, #590, #588, #1385, #1384; 3 soft or re-scoped: #732, #1708, #717) · **19 incidental-only** (18 issues + PR #2305) · **53 with no dependency** (the 48 plus the three GCP/Purview-scoped items already counted above… see note).

Note on the last count: to keep the arithmetic exact, 10 + 19 + 53 = 82, where the 53 are the 48 issues with no mention plus 5 incidental items that barely touch the platforms (#1999, #1660, #1518, #1681, #1683). Put simply, 10 items need action or a disposition before teardown and the other 72 don't.

Two ordering constraints for the teardown:
- **#588 before the Azure destroy**, because its Key Vault secret has to be deleted through the SecretStore path.
- **#590's final live E2E before `tofu destroy`.**

#2275 and #2260 can't be finished before teardown: both wait on upstream releases, and their live-verify step then falls to #2224.
